newsitem.title: USA: U.S. ban on Lebanon travel likely to stay.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ban on Lebanon travel likely to stay.

text.p: The U.S. government does not expect to lift its ban on Americans travelling to Lebanon as a result of a visit to Washington this week by Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, the State Department said on Wednesday.
Spokesman Nicholas Burns said U.S. leaders were looking forward to what he called an "important visit" by Hariri, who will hold talks Friday with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
But he said the travel ban would continue. "It's been looked at recently. And the decision's been made to keep the travel ban in place," he told a news briefing.

"I'm sure we'll hear a lot about it in the next couple of days because you know the position of the Lebanese government on this. But, our position I don't think will change in the course of this visit," Burns added.
The United States, which saw a series of American citizens kidnapped by Islamic fundamentalist groups in Lebanon in the 1980s, insists the ban is purely for security reasons.

But officials in Beirut say Lebanon is now much safer than many countries Americans are not barred from visiting. They say the ban is politically motivated to force Lebanon into a peace agreement with Israel.
In practice, U.S. authorities turn a blind eye to visits to Lebanon by tens of thousands of visits there every year by U.S. passport-holders, many of them dual nationals.

Lebanese officials say Hariri, who left Beirut Tuesday for a private visit to Paris, will discuss with Clinton ways of financing Lebanon's reconstruction programme, stalled Middle East peace talks and regional developments.

They said the talks would include plans for a meeting of a consultative group of nations being formed by the United States -- including France, the European Union, Russia and other countries -- on reconstruction financing.
Acting Finance Minister Fouad Siniora, who accompanied Hariri, has said Lebanon will ask the group for $5 billion over five years in soft loans and donations.
The group was set up under a U.S.-brokered ceasefire deal in April that ended a 17-day Israeli blitz on Lebanon which killed 200 people and caused $500 million damage.

Burns said Hariri showed during shuttle negotiations by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher to arrange the ceasefire and set up a monitoring group on the Lebanon-Israel border "that he is a very competent negotiator".
"He's someone that the Secretary, in particular, likes to work with and respects very much," Burns said.

He said the United States was looking forward to the day when Lebanon and Israel reach a peace accord. U.S. officials admit, however, that there is little chance of this before a peace deal between Israel and Syria, a prospect which they say is currently remote.
